extracted.intended_audience: general readers/students of classic literature (readers of Don Quixote)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading / extraction of prescriptive remarks and normative statements embedded in an excerpt of Cervantes' Don Quixote (fictional narrative containing comments on chivalry, poetry, and education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knights-errant: appropriate choice of adventures
rubrics_metrics.description: "Knights-errant should attempt adventures which encourage the hope of a successful issue, not those which entirely withhold it; for valour that trenches upon temerity savours rather of madness than of courage."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don Quixote (through the gentleman) distinguishes true courage from reckless temerity: an adventure should offer at least a plausible prospect of success. Attempting impossible or suicidal feats is portrayed as madness rather than chivalric valour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chivalric duties and conduct (succour and protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don Quixote claims to have 'succoured widows, protected maidens, and given aid to wives, orphans, and minors, the proper and natural duty of knights-errant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A knight-errant's moral purpose is service to the vulnerable and upholding Christian/social duties. These acts are cited as the proper measures of genuine knight-errantry and grounds for honour/fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chivalric conventions after defeat (obligations of the vanquished)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative convention: the vanquished was to be at the mercy of the victor; the victor may command the vanquished (e.g., to return home and remain for a set period), and such commands are to be obeyed as part of the 'laws of chivalry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the chivalric code depicted, victory imposes legitimate demands on the defeated (accounting, obedience, performance of penances or commitments). These procedural obligations function as normative rules of knightly behavior in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation as part of valor
rubrics_metrics.description: "He who is prepared has his battle half fought; nothing is lost by my preparing myself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readiness and practical preparation are endorsed as prudent elements of heroic conduct; bravery without preparation is implicitly foolish. This is presented as general practical counsel, not mere boastfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should be treated with respect and cultivated
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry, gentle sir, is, as I take it, like a tender young maiden of supreme beauty... She must not be touched by the buffoons, nor by the ignorant vulgar... She must on no account be offered for sale, unless, indeed, it be in heroic poems, moving tragedies, or sprightly and ingenious comedies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry ought to be guarded from vulgarity and coarse treatment; it is appropriate for serious, elevated genres (heroic poems, tragedies, comedies) and should not be prostituted to ribaldry or cheap entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's moral character influences verse
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the poet be pure in his morals, he will be pure in his verses too; the pen is the tongue of the mind..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral integrity of the poet is posited as affecting the quality/content of poetry. Writers should avoid personal attacks and indecency; critique of vice in general is legitimate, but singling out individuals or producing ribald satire is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature plus art: ideal formation of a poet
rubrics_metrics.description: "A poet is born one... At the same time... the poet by nature who calls in art to his aid will be a far better poet... nature combined with art, and art with nature, will produce a perfect poet."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both innate talent and learned craft are important: natural gift complemented by study/art produces superior poetic work. Encourages cultivation (training, knowledge) rather than relying on nature alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and parental guidance (letting inclination govern study)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is for the parents to guide them from infancy in the ways of virtue... to force them to study this or that science I do not think wise... let him pursue whatever science they may see him most inclined to."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parents should direct children toward virtue and proper conduct but not coerce specific professional or academic choices; allow a child's demonstrated inclination to guide their studies while providing moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value judgement on learning without virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: "Learning without virtue is a pearl on a dunghill."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly attainment is judged worthless if not accompanied by moral virtue; education should be paired with ethical formation.
